Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Set the rule first: nobody rates, describes or compares a body. Keep every example on the content, and check in privately with anyone whose answers suggested skipped meals, hidden use or a lot of distress.

Every student in the room

Open by saying the page centers the pressure aimed at guys, that students of any gender feel it, and that beauty standards in the feed often reflect one narrow look rather than the range of faces and bodies in the room.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Set the rule first. Say the session centers the pressure aimed at guys, and anyone can feel it. If a student starts describing a body, redirect: “What’s the video selling?”

Slide 3 · Notes

Three minutes, popcorn: “What looks or gym content shows up most in your feed?” Expect face ratings, canthal tilt, mewing, physique checks, natty or not, supplement reviews. Ask what most of them have in common, and get them to: find a flaw, then sell the fix.

Slide 4 · Notes

Four minutes. Ask students to explain the terms. Slow down on “it’s over”: some spaces sell the idea that a face decides your future, so there’s no point trying. Friendships, relationships and careers are built on far more than bone structure. Bone smashing: say plainly, don’t.

Slide 5 · Notes

Growth timing varies by years, early and late are both normal, and some guys keep filling out into their early 20s. If the guy next to you is gaining faster, timing explains a lot of it. Tongue tricks and apps don’t change the frame.

Slide 6 · Notes

Thumbs up useful, thumbs down sales pitch, flat hand not sure. Then the next slide.

The FDA doesn’t approve supplements before they’re sold; 776 had hidden drugs, and muscle products often hid steroids (Tucker et al., 2018). The FDA links SARMs to liver damage, heart attack and stroke. Steroids in teens can close growth plates early.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn how looksmaxing and muscle content find a flaw and sell a fix, what growth timing and genetics actually set, what's really in supplements and SARMs, and the boring basics that build a body. Nobody rates, describes or compares a body in the room.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • Pens
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minThe one rule, and find a flaw, sell a fix
  2. 3 minThe words you keep hearing
  3. 2 minYour body’s own clock
  4. 5 minUseful or sales pitch? One per slide
  5. 3 minWhat’s actually in the product
  6. 3 minTurn and talk, share out
  7. 6 minTyler, Nico, Aiden, the basics, close

One on one (about 15 minutes)

One on one: what's in their feed and how often they're checking (4). Growth timing and genetics (3). What they're taking or considering, without judgment, and what's really in it (4). Signs worth watching: skipped meals, panic over a missed workout, anything hidden from a doctor (4).

Before you teach
Never rate or compare.

No one rates, describes or compares their own body or anyone else's. If a student starts, redirect to the content: "What's the video selling?"

Listen for what's underneath.

Skipped meals, compensatory exercise, panic over a missed lift, or anything hidden from a doctor point toward an eating disorder or muscle dysmorphia. Follow up individually; group isn't the place to assess it.

Ask about use without alarm.

Students using supplements, SARMs or steroids will go quiet if they feel judged. Lead with what testing found is in the products; that does more than a warning.

"It's over" thinking.

Some looksmax spaces sell the idea that a face decides your future. Hopelessness tied to appearance is worth a private check-in about mood and safety.

Guys get eating disorders.

Restricting, bulking and overtraining can look like discipline, so they get missed. Say so plainly; it gives boys permission to name it.

Coaches and trainers.

The athletic trainer is a natural ally for students who are training hard. Point to them as the expert, not the stranger with the shirtless profile picture.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Any gender.

The page focuses on guys because much of the pressure targets them. Girls, nonbinary and trans students feel versions of it too, and trans students may have specific body concerns. Keep examples open.

Race and features.

Face-rating scales often treat one narrow, mostly white look as the standard. Name that the scale is invented, and that features that vary across families and ancestries aren't flaws.

Disability and bodies that don't fit the feed.

Students with disabilities, chronic illness or different body types are rarely in this content. Keep goals about what a body can do, on that student's terms.

Culture and food.

Families eat differently, and some students fast for religious reasons. Keep advice to regular meals and enough food, without judging any family's way of eating.

Money.

Supplements, coaching and gear cost money. Make the point that the basics (sleep, regular meals, coaching from a school trainer) are free.

Early and late developers.

Growth timing varies by years. A late developer can feel singled out; normalize both early and late.

What the research says

Among 2,793 students at 20 urban middle and high schools, about 35% had used protein powders or shakes and about 5% said they'd used steroids. Most muscle-building behaviors were more common in boys.

Eisenberg, Wall and Neumark-Sztainer, Pediatrics, 2012

In 912 Canadian teens and young adults, guys who often used photo filters scored higher on drive for size and on how much muscle concerns interfered with daily life.

Ganson et al., Body Image, 2024

About 2% of US men had binge eating disorder at some point in their lives.

Hudson, Hiripi, Pope and Kessler, Biological Psychiatry, 2007

An analysis of FDA warnings found 776 supplements with hidden drug ingredients; about 12% were sold for muscle building, and those most often contained synthetic steroids.

Tucker et al., JAMA Network Open, 2018

Of 44 products sold online as SARMs, only 52% contained a SARM, 39% contained a different unapproved drug, and only 41% had the amount the label claimed.

Van Wagoner et al., JAMA, 2017

The American Academy of Pediatrics supports strength training for children and teens when it's supervised and focused on technique.

Stricker et al., Pediatrics, 2020
